 Greg Norman’s driving method which he learned from Jack Nicklaus will give amateurs ‘big advantages’
 Antony Martin
 Mon 16 November 2026 12:00 GMT · 3 min read Add to Preferred Sources Photo by Simon Bruty/Anychance/Getty Images Add to Preferred Sources 
 It’s fair to say that Greg Norman and Jack Nicklaus are two of the greatest drivers of the ball ever to have graced the game. 
 Nicklaus was the longest hitter in his era, and he was pretty accurate as well with his trusted fade.
 Norman was also an elite driver of the golf ball, and he was one of the straightest and longest hitters off the tee during his prime years.
 But what was the secret to Norman’s exceptional driving of the golf ball?
 TalkingPoints Who will be Rory McIlroy's closest rival on the DP World Tour in 2027?
 He will be looking to make history with a NINTH Race to Dubai win…
 It seems as though one of the keys to his driving was implementing a very simple method used by the great Jack Nicklaus.
 Neither Norman nor Nicklaus were wrapped up in the mechanics of the golf swing. They were feel players who relied on instinct more than anything else.
 And one of the Australian’s best driving tips proves how natural his approach to the game in general was.
 Now amateur golfers can copy this golf tip as well in order to give themselves ‘big advantages’ over their competitors.
 Greg Norman’s driving method which he learned from Jack Nicklaus
 It could be argued that driving has actually now become the most important part of the game in the modern era.
 If you’re not long and decently straight off the tee, you will have almost no chance of winning on the PGA Tour.
 And it’s the same for amateur golfers, but to a different degree. If you are an amateur who is desperately trying to improve your driving of the golf ball, Norman’s tip should be perfect for you.
 Norman once explained how amateur golfers can improve their accuracy and, indeed, their distance by changing one simple thing regarding their setup.
 “ Early in my golf life I adopted Jack Nicklaus’s technique of addressing the ball with the clubhead held just above the turf rather than resting on it. I like the idea for two big reasons, “ Norman explained.
 “ First, it keeps my grip pressure constant. As you stand over a shot, you have a natural tendency to re-grip, and each time your hands shift on the club – even a fraction – it has a major effect on the outcome of the shot. Second, it promotes a very smooth one-piece takeaway with the clubhead flowing straight from the ball. This is particularly true with the driver; there will be no tendency to snap the clubhead up quickly and vertically as there can be when the club is soled.
 “ It’s also a valuable technique when your ball is perched in a precarious lie in the rough. Soling the club in such a lie can set off a chain reaction which could move the ball, incurring a penalty. By hovering the club, you not only eliminate that risk, you reduce the tendency to snag the clubface in the grass, both on the takeaway and on the way down to the ball.
 “ I must admit that not many players – pro or amateur – hover the club at address, probably because this is not an easy method to master. But if you can learn it, you’ll give yourself some big advantages over the vast majority of golfers. “ 
 The beauty of this tip from Greg Norman is that it has absolutely nothing to do with mechanics of the golf swing or technique.
 It really is as simple as it gets. If it’s good enough for Greg Norman and Jack Nicklaus, it should be good enough for us!
